name: gputaskman
works_with: Windows with NVIDIA, AMD or Intel GPUs, Linux and WSL, and macOS on Apple Silicon
short: A terminal task manager for your GPU that shows which process uses how much VRAM, and what an LLM's weights and KV cache take.
what: gputaskman is a terminal UI that ties per-process GPU memory and activity to the runtimes and model files each process has loaded. For local LLMs it can break memory down into weights, KV cache and compute buffers, and it shows hints from Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp servers. It also prints one-shot text or JSON snapshots and can record a session.
who: People running local AI models, games or GPU work who want to know what is filling their VRAM. Skip it if your workloads run in the cloud or only on the CPU or NPU, which it does not cover. The author calls it early, experimental software.
needs: Python 3.11+ with uv or pipx, or the portable Windows or Linux build
A supported GPU and driver: a current WDDM driver on Windows, an NVIDIA driver (or AMD `amdgpu` or Intel `i915` on native Linux) on Linux
glibc 2.35 or newer for the portable Linux builds
A wide terminal, roughly 140 columns, for the full table

steps.title: Install from PyPI
steps.text: No clone is needed. The shorter `gtm` command also works.

steps.title: Or run the portable Windows build
steps.text: Download the ZIP for your PC from the Releases page and extract the entire ZIP, keeping `_internal` beside `gputaskman.exe`. No Python is needed.

steps.title: Or run the portable Linux build
Find your way around
steps.text: Use Up and Down to inspect a process, `s` to change the sort, `m` for slim or full mode, `?` to explain the counters and `q` to quit.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Load a local model, then run `gputaskman --json` before and after and compare the two files with `gputaskman diff before.json after.json`.

watch: The inspector and JSON output can contain paths, command lines, model names and local ports. Check and redact them before you post a capture.
Classifications and GGUF-based breakdowns are estimates. Only the device and process counters are measurements.
On Linux, other users' processes need `sudo`. On macOS, measuring every process's memory also needs `sudo`.
It says it sends no telemetry and does not dump model weights.
